sentences.text: Stratiotosuchus possessed a robust, laterally compressed skull measuring 47 cm in length, making it one of the largest known baurusuchids.
Its teeth were ziphodont, a term describing structures that are laterally compressed, curved, and serrated.
Unlike most baurusuchids which typically have four premaxillary teeth, the holotype of Stratiotosuchus — the specimen the species is based on — possessed only three.
This animal stood with a fully erect posture similar to that of bipedal theropod dinosaurs.
Preparation of the holotype skeleton revealed evidence of two individuals preserved together in the same sandstone block.
The upper part of the femur features a rough surface region analogous to the accessory trochanter found in tetanuran theropods.
The articular surface where the tibia attaches to the femur is laterally compressed, unlike the circular surface in living crocodilians but similar to theropod dinosaurs.
The first fossils of Stratiotosuchus were found in the 1980s, and the type species was named in 2001.
Stratiotosuchus was described by Campos and colleagues in 2001.
Stratiotosuchus was a hyperpredator that likely filled ecological niches occupied by theropod dinosaurs in other regions.
Large crests over its hip socket stabilized the hip in a pillar-erect stance.
It likely had a much stronger puboischiotibialis muscle than modern crocodilians, allowing it to maintain a permanent upright stance.
The arm socket faced backwards and downwards, suggesting its arms were held beneath the body.
Tightly clustered metacarpals forming narrow hands and a backward-projecting calcaneal tuberosity suggest an erect posture.
Stratiotosuchus is classified in the class Reptilia.
It belongs to the clade Metasuchia, which includes living crocodilians and extinct relatives extending back into the Jurassic.
The animal belongs to the family Baurusuchidae.
Its parent group is Baurusuchinae.
According to Montefeltro et al. (2011), Stratiotosuchus belongs to the subfamily Baurusuchinae within the family Baurusuchidae.
Riff and Kellner (2011) placed Stratiotosuchus deep within Notosuchia as the sister taxon to the family Sphagesauridae.
Stratiotosuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous.
Specimens come from the Adamantina Formation, which dates to either the Turonian-Santonian (about 85 million years ago) or the Campanian-Maastrichtian (about 70 million years ago).
Stratiotosuchus lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
The exact phylogenetic position of Stratiotosuchus within the clade Metasuchia remains uncertain.
